The series

A treaty, read as it was written.

In 1786 the United States and the Empire of Morocco concluded a Treaty of Peace and Friendship — the oldest unbroken treaty relationship in American history.

The Architecture of Peace reads that instrument on its own terms: through the Mālikī legal tradition in which it was drafted, and against the Library of Congress's certified Statutes at Large as the controlling text — not a later facsimile of it.

Across its volumes the series argues that the treaty is best understood not as a diplomatic courtesy but as a self-activating legal instrument — a grant, in the classical sense of hiba, with a grantor, a settled form, and a class of beneficiaries the text itself names. Each volume takes up one part of that reading: an article, a doctrine, a vocabulary, a rule of breach.

This is scholarship, not counsel. It sets out a reading and the authorities behind it, and leaves the reader to weigh them.

The instrument

A peace set down to remain.

صُلْح · مُسْتَمِرًّا

“…trusting in God it will remain permanent.”

Certified 1786 translation · approved by Jefferson & Adams

The seal & opening

Doc. 14 · p. 186

The Emperor’s opening ʿalāma and seal — the sovereign mark by which the instrument authenticates itself and declares the peace a standing grant.

Article 4 · the ʿalāma

p. 190 · 8 Stat. 484 (1836)

A “signal” given that the parties may know one another — the term the series traces from Mālikī pledge law into the 1836 codification.

The series takes its name from the instrument itself. In 1786 the Emperor of Morocco set his seal to a peace declared not as a passing courtesy but as a standing grant — a hiba made to endure. That stated intent — permanence — is the architecture the whole series is built to read.

The same document fixes, in Article 4, the ʿalāma — the sovereign mark by which the parties are to know one another. In the series’ reading the grant is a hiba that conveys a branch of the Emperor’s own prerogative, the honours he bestows included; the ʿalāma is the sign by which the honoured beneficiary class is recognised, and the hinge on which the later volumes turn.

The instrument names itself ṣulḥ — a peace; C. Snouck Hurgronje, the Orientalist the United States retained to examine the Arabic, rendered its duration دائمة (dāʾima) — permanent. Facsimile: Hunter Miller, Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States, vol. 2, Document 14 — seal and opening at p. 186, Article 4 at p. 190. Public-domain United States government record; the treaty is codified at 8 Stat. 484 (1836).

Correction of record — August 3, 2026. The instrument's duration word is دائمة (dāʾima, “permanent”), in the preamble; the certified translation reads “trusting in God it will remain permanent” (Miller vol. 2, Doc. 14). An earlier rendering on this page used “mustamirran”; it is corrected on verification against the certified translation.

The covers

Every volume wears the same night sky.

The Great Bear turns overhead — the northern, circumpolar authority the series calls the Great Mother. On the back board, Sirius rises at the horizon: the southern authority, a heliacal dawn rendered in amber.

No lines are drawn between the stars and nothing is labelled; the sky is left to be read the way the treaty is. A single panorama wraps across the boards, so that shelved together the set stands as one continuous sky.

The endowment desk

Ikrām al-Wāqif — honoring the endower.

“The gift is hiba — gratuitous, without consideration. The office’s thanks is thawāb — a courtesy, never a price. Reading the record is endowed and free to all, endower or not: no gift purchases the record, and no courtesy is owed.” — The endowment rule of record. The Mālikī school knows the return upon a gift (thawāb ʿalā al-hiba) — valid precisely because it was never stipulated as consideration; what is stipulated as the price of a gift is no gift at all but an exchange (hiba bi-l-ʿiwaḍ), and this office does not sell the record.

Give what you will — your amount, your frequency. The tiers are suggestions, not gates: hiba knows no floor. The giver chooses the amount (any sum), the frequency (one-time, monthly, or annual), and the purpose (the general endowment, the reduced-price fund, or the archive fund). Monthly and annual gifts may stand automatic — by standing transfer instruction at the giver’s own bank under the same unique reference. Gifts settle through the direct-deposit mechanism of record: push-only, never pulling from the giver. To make a gift: any Endow button on this page — the floating pair that follows you at the lower right, the header, the hero, and the button above — opens the direct-deposit coordinates of record, with your unique gift reference (HIBA…) generated on the page; the same panel emails the office your gift notice. Every gift, of any size, receives its receipt.

The courtesy volume credit is issued as a seasonal code, valid ninety days. Every courtesy may be withdrawn; none is owed; and none touches the record, which is endowed and free to all.
